h.select_rule: Discard any hypothesis whose condition is the edited field's own current value, or whose condition merely disables or disconnects the edited component. From the rest, keep 10 with distinct mechanisms and field pairs, favouring those where an informed expert could plausibly bet on either direction.
h.strategy: Two patterns are banned because experts find them obvious: (1) conditioning on the current value of the same field being edited, which just restates that upgrading a weak setting helps more than upgrading a strong one; (2) conditions that make the edited component unused, unreachable or inert. Instead, each hypothesis must link two DIFFERENT fields that interact through a non-trivial mechanism, such as substitution between parallel routes, a capacity already supplied elsewhere, one part acting as a bottleneck for another, or interference that turns a usually helpful edit harmful. No condition setting may appear in more than two hypotheses. Use the gaps and negated assumptions as the source of each idea. In each 'why', name the mechanism and explain why the opposite direction is also a priori plausible.

hyps.why: sklearn scales the L2 gradient by 1/batch_size per step, so small batches get roughly N/B^2 decay per epoch and extra alpha over-shrinks the weights.
Under standard parametrisation with Adam, wider layers produce larger function changes per step, which compensates for a too-small learning rate.
Wide layers sum many fan-in updates, so a larger Adam step overshoots more easily.
Large batches give few updates in 243 epochs, and deeper nets need more steps to train, so the update budget becomes a bottleneck.
Strong L2 shrinkage compounds multiplicatively across stacked weight matrices, starving deeper nets of signal.
Per-layer update errors compound through a deeper stack, lowering the maximum stable learning rate.
At low LR a deep stack cannot finish training in 243 epochs, so removing a layer relieves an optimisation bottleneck.
With one hidden layer, width is the only source of capacity, whereas deeper nets already gain capacity from depth, so width has diminishing returns there.
Larger batches reduce gradient variance and stabilise training that is near divergence at high learning rates.
Large batches yield few updates in 243 epochs, so a bigger step is needed to make progress within the fixed budget.
